analysis.one_liner: Starts the post-Congress lobbying ban clock at the end of a member's elected term, not their early exit.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law bars former senators from lobbying Congress for 2 years and former House members for 1 year after they leave office. This bill would move the starting point to the end of the term the member was elected to serve. So a member who resigns early — say, mid-term, to take a lobbying job — would still be barred until the full term ran out, closing a path that lets departing members start lobbying sooner.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people get a slightly stronger revolving-door rule: a member who quits Congress mid-term could not immediately cash in on a lobbying career, because the ban would run until the term they were elected to serve actually expires. It also modestly protects the integrity of the lobbying disclosure system by removing an incentive to resign early for a lobbying job [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public, via a stronger revolving-door rule

how_it_helps.text: It closes a timing loophole: a senator who resigns, or is appointed and leaves, before their term ends would face a 2-year lobbying ban that starts when the term expires, not when they walk out the door [S2].
House members who leave before their term ends would face a 1-year ban starting at term expiration, so quitting early would no longer shorten the wait before lobbying Congress [S2].
It applies to anyone leaving the House or Senate on or after enactment, so current and future members are covered [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Former members of Congress who want to move into lobbying sooner, and the lobbying firms and trade groups that hire them — mainly in cases where a member leaves office before the term they were elected to serve has run out. Members themselves bear a longer waiting period before taking a lobbying job [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Former members and the lobbying firms that hire them

drawbacks.text: The ban length does not change — 2 years for senators, 1 for House members — and the bill does nothing about the well-known workarounds, such as taking a 'strategic adviser' job that falls outside the legal definition of lobbying, so its practical effect is narrow [S2].

The new clock can stretch a ban well beyond two years: a senator who resigns halfway through a six-year term could be barred from lobbying for roughly five years, which supporters would call the point but which is a real cost to the individual's career [S2].
With zero cosponsors, the bill had no visible coalition behind it, and the House never gave it any consideration beyond referral [S3][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea is sound — a member elected to a six-year term should not be able to shorten the lobbying ban by resigning early — but the bill is a small patch. It leaves the ban's length untouched and does not address the larger revolving-door problem: former officials can work as influencers, consultants, or coalition-builders without ever registering as lobbyists. The cost is borne only by departing members and the firms that want to hire them, which is exactly who the bill targets.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never took it up before the congressional term ended, so it died quietly.

narrative.text: Rep. Claudia Tenney introduced the Don't Quit to Lobby Act on April 11, 2024 [S1][S4].
The same day, the House referred it to the Judiciary Committee, the standard first step that puts a bill in a committee's hands [S4].
No other action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and the bill attracted zero cosponsors before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Former members of Congress and the lobbying industry are better off, because the existing rule still lets a member who leaves office early start lobbying before the term they were elected to serve is over. No one in the public lost anything concrete, but the modest ethics fix on the table is gone.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Former members and the lobbying industry

for.name: Rep. Claudia Tenney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee; it was her bill alone.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it died there when the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no party position can be read from the record; the sponsor was a Republican.

industries.industry: Lobbying firms and government relations shops
industries.note: The bill would delay when former members can join these firms and lobby their former colleagues, shrinking the pipeline of fresh ex-Congress hires in early-resignation cases. Because the bill died, nothing changed for them.

industries.industry: Former members of Congress (the revolving door itself)
industries.note: Departing members would have lost the option of quitting mid-term to shorten their cooling-off period. The waiting period before monetizing a congressional career would run to the end of the elected term.
